transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-10 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Acme), Sara Gomez (Acme), Marcus Chen (Acme)

Summary: Quick scoping call for a POC focused on data handling requirements: PII redaction, logging & retention, prompt storage, KMS/encryption, and benchmark success criteria. Agreed to run an initial benchmark with anonymized prompts and confirm retention/KMS approach.

Topics: data retention, prompt storage, redaction, logging levels, encryption/KMS, benchmarks (latency/throughput), timeline for POC

00:00 Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro, we're here to scope the POC around data handling for the inference pipeline, specifically around PII and retention
00:12 Jordan: yep, thanks, main ask from Acme is we can't have raw PII persisted offsite, also need audit logs and proof of deletion for regulators
00:25 Priya: totally understood. quick question about what you mean by raw PII — are you seeing names, SSNs, account numbers in prompts or in user-uploaded docs?
00:34 Marcus: mostly user-entered prompts and some attachments. prompts can contain names and account ids occasionally, attachments we'll scope separately
00:50 Sara: regulators expect logs for access but we need the ability to redact or keep hashed prompts, and retention of logs for 90 days but PII removed after 7 days ideally
01:05 Alex: fine. on Redwood side we have options: hosted API with prompt logging disabled, or use our private/Dedicated offering where prompt storage can be configured to never persist prompts, or persist encrypted with customer KMS keys. we can also run a proxy redaction step before sending to models
01:25 Jordan: can you walk through the redaction options and where it happens? client side? our side? within Redwood?
01:40 Priya: yes, three main patterns: 1) client-side redaction — customer strips PII before sending. 2) Redwood-side redaction — we run a redaction preprocessor in the request path (can be configured to not store originals). 3) Post-processing with hashed pointers — we hash the prompt and store only hash for traceability. note transcription: sometimes our notes say K-V cache or KV cash -- we mean KV cache for model state
02:12 Sara: if you do Redwood-side redaction, do you ever keep the original prompt in any log for troubleshooting?
02:20 Priya: default for hosted is we log minimal request metadata but you can opt out and choose no prompt persistence. for Dedicated/Private you can set retention to zero for prompts; for hosted we also offer customer-managed KMS so even if persisted it's encrypted with your key
02:40 Marcus: what's the time to erase? we need proof we can delete content on demand
02:46 Alex: we support programmatic deletion via an API and an audit trail; for Dedicated we can do immediate purge. for hosted, we can set retention windows (e.g., 7/30/90 days) and provide deletion job records
03:05 Jordan: ok, how does this affect our ability to run benchmarks and reproduce issues? we need traces to debug latency/regressions
03:15 Priya: good point. recommended approach: keep a hashed copy of prompts plus request IDs and save a small debug snapshot for a limited window (e.g., 7 days) that you control. snapshots can be disabled after benchmark window. hashes allow mapping back only if you keep original mapping locally
03:40 Sara: and what about streaming responses and logs — do response tokens ever get stored?
03:47 Alex: by default we stream to the client and don't persist full responses unless configured. if you need transcripts for quality evaluation we recommend sending eval data to a separate secure bucket with your KMS key and short retention
04:05 Jordan: encryption — you said customer KMS is supported for hosted. is HSM or bring-your-own-key in scope?
04:12 Priya: yes, we support customer-managed KMS for hosted and Dedicated; for Private we can integrate HSM/HSM-backed KMS depending on deployment. note: some cloud KMSs have export restrictions, we'll document supported providers
04:28 Marcus: any SOC2/ISO attestations? auditors will ask
04:32 Alex: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II in scope, we have ISO docs and can share the pack. we'll include audit log examples in the docs we send
04:45 Jordan: benchmark success criteria — we want to see p95 latency below 250ms for 32-token completions and stable throughput of 50 reqs/s with less than 5% error rate for the POC workload
04:59 Priya: noted. we'll propose a benchmark plan: run 4-hour steady load + 1-hour ramp tests, plus cold-start tests for a simulated 1k user concurrency spread. we will instrument token-level latency, batching efficiency, and KV cache hit rates
05:18 Marcus: for cost evaluation, we need per-token breakdown and examples for batching benefits
05:24 Alex: Redwood Optimize will produce an estimate; for POC we'll run a sample 24-hour sim to estimate unit costs and provide recommendations (quantization, batching config)
05:36 Sara: legal will insist on a data processing agreement and deletion SLA
05:41 Alex: yes we'll share standard DPA and can discuss tighter SLAs for Dedicated or Private deployments in the enterprise package
05:52 Jordan: timeline — we want a 6-week POC, starting as soon as docs and sample data are shared; first two weeks focus on security and config, next two on benchmarks, final two on validation and handoff
06:06 Priya: timeline sounds reasonable. immediate next steps: Alex sends security pack; Jordan provides anonymized prompts and PII rules; Priya prepares bench scripts
06:18 Sara: question on prompt storage: can you store prompts hashed and still do quality evals? we need to see actual prompts sometimes for root cause
06:26 Priya: yes, you can keep local mapping (customer) from hash to prompt for deep-dive only. Redwood can store only the hash and a small eval snippet (masking PII) for a short window
06:40 Jordan: will Redwood run redaction models or do we supply regex rules?
06:45 Priya: both. we have a config that supports regex-based redaction and an ML-based PII detector (less perfect but better recall). for regulated fields we recommend deterministic redaction via patterns plus post-check ML filter
06:59 Marcus: are there any limitations on attachments in the POC? sensitive docs are out of scope for hosted?
07:05 Alex: attachments with PHI or PII we recommend Private or Dedicated. for hosted we can accept attachments if you use client-side redaction or send through our Private pipeline
07:18 Jordan: ok. can we see an example audit log entry?
07:21 Alex: yes we'll include a sample in the pack. it includes request id, timestamp, model variant, token counts, action (ingest, delete), and retention tag, but not the full prompt if you opt-out
07:34 Sara: one more — do you support SSO & RBAC so only certain roles can request deletion?
07:40 Alex: yes SSO/SAML and RBAC available; deletion actions are logged and require proper role permissions
07:46 Priya: to summarize the POC success criteria you mentioned: 1) security: no raw PII persisted offsite, deletion SLA met; 2) performance: p95 < 250ms for 32 tokens and throughput 50 reqs/s; 3) cost: per-token cost within expected range from Redwood estimate; 4) reproducibility: ability to debug with hashed prompts and limited snapshots
08:10 Jordan: that matches our internal charter. if redaction affects model quality we'll accept a small delta but want guardrails
08:18 Priya: we'll include eval prompts to measure quality delta pre/post redaction, and quantify impact in the bench report
08:28 Alex: final recap of next steps and owners — see action items. we'll set the next meeting to kick off benchmarks once Jordan uploads the sample corpus
08:37 Marcus: sounds good, thanks everyone
08:40 Sara: thanks
08:42 Alex: thanks, we'll follow up by EOD with the docs

End of transcript
